approachQuestion.prompt: A monitoring system stores readings in several individually ordered runs. Merge them into one nondecreasing array, preserving every occurrence. A run may be empty. Example 1: runs=[[1,4,9],[1,3,10],[2,2,8]] → [1,1,2,2,3,4,8,9,10]. Example 2: runs=[[],[-3,0,0],[2]] → [-3,0,0,2]. What approach produces the merged array?
constraints: 1 ≤ m ≤ 100000 runs; let N be the total number of readings across all runs, with 0 ≤ N ≤ 300000.
Each run is already sorted in nondecreasing order. Readings are signed 64-bit integers; comparisons take constant time.
Do not modify the runs. The output contains all N readings, including duplicates.
A run can be empty; when all runs are empty, return an empty array.

options.text: Place the first unread reading from each nonempty run in a min-oriented priority queue, recording its run. Repeatedly remove the smallest reading, append it to the output, and insert the next reading from that same run if one remains.
options.feedback: The queue contains only the current smallest unread candidate from each run. Since each run is ordered, no later reading in a run can precede its current head.

options.text: Keep one current position per run. For every output value, inspect the current reading of every nonempty run, append the smallest one, and advance only that run.
options.feedback: This produces the right order and uses the fact that only current run heads can be next. However, it rescans those heads for every output instead of maintaining the current best candidate, so the same active runs are repeatedly reconsidered.

options.text: Copy all readings into one array, sort that array, and return it.
options.feedback: This preserves every occurrence and gives the correct order, but it ignores that each input run is already ordered. The runs can be combined by considering only their current unread heads.

options.text: Merge adjacent runs two at a time using the standard two-pointer merge, then merge the resulting runs in further rounds until one remains.
options.feedback: This is correct and uses the existing order, but each round writes intermediate merged runs. The current-head method can emit directly to the final output while tracking one candidate per nonempty run.

feedback.reason: Focus on how many candidates must remain available after each new value arrives, and what the requested result requires you to retain.
details: Keep one candidate for each nonempty run: its first unread reading. Repeatedly choose the smallest candidate, append it to the result, and replace it with the next reading from that same run. Stop when no candidates remain.

The smallest unread item of each sorted run is its only possible next contribution. Advancing the selected run preserves that frontier. Empty runs still cost initial inspection, even when total output N is zero.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze the fixed method: inspect all m runs, collect the first reading from every nonempty run, and build a min-oriented priority queue from those entries using bottom-up heap construction. Until the queue is empty, remove its smallest entry, append that reading to the output, and insert the next reading from the same run when available. Let N be the total number of readings and m the number of input runs.
constraints: Use worst-case bounds. Queue insertion and removal restore heap order; comparing two readings and moving one reading take constant time.
The returned N-element array is output and is excluded from auxiliary space. The input runs are excluded; count the queue, run/index bookkeeping, and other working storage.

options.text: O(m + N log(m+1)) time, O(m) auxiliary space
O(N + m) time, O(m) auxiliary space
O(N log N) time, O(N) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Inspect m runs, then repair an at-most-m heap for each emitted reading.
details: All m runs are inspected, and bottom-up heap construction takes O(m) time. Each of the N readings is removed once and, except for the first reading of its run, inserted once; each queue operation costs O(log(m+1)) in the worst case. The queue and run/index bookkeeping use O(m) space, even when some runs are empty. The returned array is excluded. This bound is tight: with m≥2 nonempty runs each of length L≥2, let run j contain t·m+j for t=0…L−1 and j=0…m−1. After the initial Θ(m) scan/build, Θ(N) outputs each advance a run to a key greater than all other current heads; root replacement descends Θ(log m) levels, giving Θ(N log m). The queue contains m heads, so its worst-case auxiliary storage is Θ(m). For m=1, each of N outputs uses a one-entry queue, giving Θ(N), while inspecting the run costs Θ(m); for N=0, the initial scan still costs Θ(m).

“O(N + m) time, O(m) auxiliary space”: The method performs heap removals and insertions as it advances through the runs. Counting only one constant-time action per reading omits queue reordering, although the initial run scan is linear.
“O(N log N) time, O(N) auxiliary space”: The fixed method does not copy and sort all readings. Its queue tracks run heads, so its working state depends on the number of nonempty runs, not on N.
“O(Nm) time, O(m) auxiliary space”: The method does not inspect all m runs for every output. It removes the globally smallest current head directly from the priority queue.
